content:
Earlier, I replaced a battery-powered push mower with a robotic mower that can be controlled via iPhone. Users need to manually drive the mower around the yard using their iPhone to establish a virtual map. Once set up, the machine will automatically carry out mowing tasks according to a preset schedule.

Recently, I tried another system called the TerraMow V1000. It uses a completely different navigation method, and after several weeks of testing, I think it might be an easier choice for many people.

Camera-driven automatic mapping

The biggest difference between the TerraMow V1000 and the Anthbot M9 I tested earlier this year lies in how each machine understands your yard.

The Anthbot M9 uses an RTK base station for positioning. During setup, I had to manually drive the mower along the boundary using my iPhone to create the initial map.

On the other hand, the TerraMow V1000 uses a system the company calls TerraVision 2.0. Three cameras allow the mower to automatically map the lawn, with no need to install boundary wires beforehand, and no extra RTK antenna required.

Automatic initial mapping takes longer. However, I think this method may be easier for users who are less familiar with technology.

To verify this, I specifically asked my mother, who lives in another state, to set up and use the TerraMow V1000 on her own, without any help from me. She replied that everything worked fine. But I'm not entirely sure she would have had the patience to manually drive the robot along the entire boundary and then manually mark out areas to avoid.

Automatic mapping ran into a few hiccups in my front yard. There's no fence or other physical separation between my lawn and my neighbour's, so TerraMow initially included part of my neighbour's lawn in my map.

I solved the problem by marking that area as a no-go zone in the app. However, if a lawn doesn't have clear visual boundaries, the initial mapping process may require a bit more effort.

Viewing through the mower's cameras

TerraMow's cameras also support one of my favourite features. The iPhone app can show in real time what the mower sees while it's working.

During testing, I used the iPhone Mirroring feature on my Mac to open this view in a large window. That way I could work indoors while watching from the robot's first-person perspective as it navigated the backyard.

This feature isn't essential for automatic mowing, but it makes the robot more fun to use and occasionally explains why it slows down or avoids certain objects. The Anthbot M9 doesn't have a similar camera view feature.

Beyond that, the two iPhone apps share many similar design elements. Both allow you to schedule jobs, adjust mowing behaviour, divide zones, mark areas to avoid, and remotely control the mower.

Speaking of that last feature, TerraMow has a particularly clever touch. In addition to the usual left and right virtual joysticks, its app also offers a one-handed mode. You can hold your iPhone normally and use your thumb to control the mower.

Manually driving the mower with your iPhone isn't the main purpose of either system. Ideally, the robot should be able to complete its work automatically based on a preset schedule, without human intervention. That said, TerraMow's joystick controls proved surprisingly useful for tidying up spots it had missed.

Sometimes, I almost felt like I was controlling the robot with telekinesis (a wonderful feeling). I could let my iPhone hang at my side while walking, and with just a slight nudge of my thumb, the machine would drive towards me.

Every robotic mower app should copy this control method.

A more aggressive mower

Overall, the TerraMow V1000 feels more aggressive than the Anthbot M9. During testing, it cut lower and was noticeably louder while working.

I wouldn't call TerraMow loud. But the difference between the two is obvious. The Anthbot can run so quietly that you almost forget it's still mowing, even when it's working at night with its headlights on.

Because TerraMow relies on cameras for navigation, it needs daylight to operate reliably. That makes daytime scheduling more important.

The V1000 itself feels solid and is also larger than the Anthbot M9. TerraMow includes a protective garage that can cover the charging dock, while Anthbot's garage has to be purchased separately.

Most importantly, the TerraMow has been consistently stable and reliable. I relied on it to mow for several weeks in a row, during which I never had to intervene personally.

When adaptive mapping is too clever

The same kind of visual intelligence that makes TerraMow easy to set up can sometimes backfire.

The mower continually updates its map based on what it sees. Saving these updates after each job takes some time, during which you can't do anything else in the app.

After several days of rain, I ran into an interesting special case. A puddle appeared in part of the yard, and TerraMow cleverly avoided that area during its next run.

The grass inside the circular area it had skipped started growing taller. As time went on, the mower seemed to treat that patch of tall grass as something to keep avoiding, and even after the ground had dried, that patch of grass was consistently excluded from its working area.

I used the app's remote control feature to manually drive the mower over that tall grass and cut it. Once that area returned to normal lawn condition, automatic mowing resumed there as usual.

Regular edging can also help TerraMow approach boundaries more confidently. If the grass in areas with unclear boundaries grows too tall, the system may treat it as an obstacle rather than part of the mowing area.

Anthbot's approach feels less adaptive and relies more heavily on boundaries and obstacles set by the user. That method requires more upfront work, but it avoids situations where the map "changes its mind" about a patch of grass.

9to5Mac's take

After using both systems, for most people I tend to recommend TerraMow's camera-based approach.

For me, laying boundary wires beforehand is completely out of the question, and installing an RTK base station means having one more piece of hardware to position, power, and maintain. TerraMow requires neither.

Its visual navigation isn't flawless. Initial mapping takes longer, an invisible property line requires manual correction, and its adaptive behaviour once mistook tall grass for a permanent obstacle.

All of these issues are manageable. In return, the TerraMow V1000 offers simpler setup, reliable automatic mowing, excellent real-time camera views, and the best manual controls I've ever seen in a robotic mower app.

I personally really enjoy yard work, but mowing is the most repetitive part. Handing this task over to a robot frees up more time for me to focus on landscaping, edging, and detailed work, while keeping the lawn neat.

The TerraMow V1000 performs well enough for me to recommend it, especially for those who want robotic mowing but don't want the hassle of laying wires, installing an RTK antenna, or manually walking the entire yard with an iPhone.

Amazon currently prices the TerraMow V1000 at US$999, and a US$200 coupon is available for use on the website. You can also find the product on TerraMow's official website.
